title: LOUISVILLE VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Louisville Village Board met Thursday evening and made quick work of a light agenda.

After Mayor Chris Rinehart called the meeting to order, trustees not only approved the meeting agenda but also the past meeting minutes and the bills.

In regular business, the mayor asked the board to consider the agreement for the care of the pocket park on the courthouse square for next year.  The village is seeking to continue paying Donna Frutiger $300 per month to care for the appearance of the pocket for the months of April through December.  A motion was made to approve his request and trustees voted 4-2 in favor.  Trustees Chuck Smith and Scott Ikemire voted against and later stated that they believe that amount is too much to pay for the upkeep of the pocket park.

Next, Mayor Rinehart introduced a discussion topic of creating an ordinance to ban shipping containers within the village to be used as storage facilities.  Rinehart said that after some earlier discussions about the topic, he was asking if anyone wanted to adopt a policy either banning the practice altogether or to enact regulations on their use.  With no one making motion, the issue was tabled, at least for the time being.

The main issue of the meeting was a discussion about the need for a new mower for village properties.  Utilities Superintendent Troy Elwood said that since he began his duties in Louisville, they hadn’t purchased a new mower but had bought used ones.  He stated that there are continuing issues in some areas with quick overgrowth during rainy periods along fences and in certain locations like mowing around the sloped village sewer lagoon levees.  Elwood said he and the mayor were considering moving up from a simple mower to a more rugged sub compact tractor.  He explained they were considering John Deere models including an X750 and a 1025R.  Each had pros and cons with varying attachments offered as part of a package deal for the tractor and better pricing on the mower.  One of the main issues was the clearance space under the mowing deck.  He explained that the areas they mow are not flat, well-manicured lawns, but sloped uneven ground where a riding lawn mower deck can suddenly stop when it  bottoms out and frequently causes a drive belt to break.  A sub compact tractor has a higher clearance and can better handle uneven ground.  The board considered quotes from Sydenstricker Nobbe Partners in Flora and Sloan Implement in Effingham.  In the end, trustees voted unanimously to approve the purchase of the X750 Mower from Sloan Implement at a price of $12,650.

Next, the mayor asked the board to consider two TIF Façade Grant requests.  The village reimburses businesses for half of what they spend on making improvements to the exterior of their buildings, up to a maximum of $5,000 for a $10,000 project.  The first was for the Clay County Republican Newspaper building at 126 S. Church Street.  Following a brief discussion, members voted to reimburse up to the maximum of $5,000 for repairs to Smitty’s building.  The second request was from Sonja Harrison for her business Visible Changes at 148 S. Church Street.  Trustees voted to approve a total of $1,747.50 of the $3,495 total.

As the meeting continued, Mayor Rinehart noted that the FY2027 Budget is now available for public inspection and will lay open for 30 days before it is adopted at the May meeting, preceded by a public hearing to allow for discussion.

The board then took up the issue of a pay raise for all village employees.  Trustees made quick work of it when Scott Ikemire made a motion to give employees a 4% raise, and fellow members quickly approved that amount.

That was followed by short discussion on the topic of mowing bids.  There were two bids, one by Ronald Coble and the other by Brian Wattles.  Coble’s bid was accepted for the K-1 property, the old water tower, the property on Tanner and the ditch on Hayes Street.  Wattles bid was accepted for mowing the cemetery across from North Clay High School.

There was also a brief discussion about the possibility of issuing an expanded liquor license for Casey’s General Store.  Village Attorney Kyle Boose pointed out that in order to add hard liquor, a new class of license would need to be created, or they could expand their Class B license.  He noted that in either situation it would need to be delayed until a future meeting.  In the end, no action was taken.

In open time, it was suggested that the board take up mowing bids in March rather than April so that they wouldn’t have to wait to get started with the mowing season if warm weather starts early.  There was also a short mention of seeking grants for improvements to Louisville streets, however it was said by Engineer Brandon Bridges, of Charleston Engineering, that information was not ready yet.  Utilities Superintendent Troy Elwood also stated that the village is now taking applications for summer employment.  The positions are for maintenance/labor/office positions.  The length of employment is yet to be determined but will be less than 1,000 hours and will pay minimum wage.  Resumes’ and applications must be received at the Louisville Village Hall by 4:00pm on May 8th.

title: NO BODY TO MURDER
full_story:
A play titled “No Body to Murder” will be held at Nostalgia Theater, formerly the Town Theater, in downtown Flora this weekend.  The play will be held tonight, and tomorrow night, at 7 pm.  This fun whodunnit takes place on a stormy night and will have you laughing along and keep you guessing.  This is a stage performance, not a murder mystery event and there will be no audience participation.

The play is directed by Stacey Earleywine and is full of amazing local talent, who will blow you away with their acting abilities.  Although this play is not a musical, it is full of great songs in between scenes.

Grab a friend and enjoy an evening out with well-known community theater members Jeremy Kohn, Jim Earleywine, Matt Lovett, Jessica Muskopf, Linda Waller, Sarah Hager, and more.

Nostalgia Theater is currently being renovated and will serve as Clay County’s home for community theater.  Not only will you be able to catch some amazing live entertainment at Nostalgia, but the building is also for rent as a venue for upcoming events, such as parties, reunions, showers, and weddings.

Nostalgia Theater operates as a 501©3 non-profit and all proceeds from the Nostalgia play performances will be used to continue the renovation of the theater.  Make plans to attend this fun performance, support the hard work these actors have put into it, and see the beautiful Nostalgia Theater building as it is being brought back to life.

title: WAYNE CITY WELFARE CHECK
full_story:
On Monday at approximately 9:17pm, Wayne County Sheriff’s Deputies responded to a rural Wayne City residence to conduct a welfare check on two juvenile children.

The caller advised they were on the phone with one of the juveniles and the juvenile stated “why are you hitting me.”  Deputies began searching for the two juveniles and their mother Cynthia Solomon, 37, of Wayne City.  After making phone contact with Solomon she lied about her location.  After a lengthy search Deputies located one of the juveniles walking on Route 242 South of Wayne City.  The juvenile stated that their mother Solomon had become angry and began battering them and throwing items at them including a laptop computer.  The juvenile stated that Solomon made them get into the vehicle with her and told them that they were going to die tonight.  A short time into the trip the juvenile asked how they would die and she kicked them out of the vehicle and stated they were going to be left in the roadway to be hit by a semi-truck.  Solomon then left one juvenile in the road and continued on with one juvenile still in the vehicle.

A short time later Deputies located Solomon and the second juvenile and took Solomon into custody.  Solomon remains in the Wayne County Jail.  The case is continuing with the Wayne County Sheriff’s Office and DCFS.

Cynthia Solomon faces charges of Domestic Battery, Endangering the life and health of a child, and Obstructing justice.

title: NORTH WAYNE PRESCHOOL SCREENING
full_story:
The North Wayne Schools are conducting Child Find/Preschool screening for three to five-year-old children not yet enrolled in public schools and who will not be Kindergarten eligible in the fall.

The screening checks each child’s progress in hearing, vision, speech, language, and coordination skills.  This will give parents a better idea of how their child is progressing at this very young age before he/she begins school.  This screening program is free, and parents will receive immediate feedback on how their child is developing.  Head Start personnel may also be present to explain their program and services.

The Child Find/Preschool Screening will be held at Johnsonville on April 20th, from 8:30 am to 2:30 pm.  The screening procedure takes about 45 minutes, and appointments must be made so that children do not have a long wait period.  Parents should call 618-673-3044 to make an appointment or to get more information.

The service is a free check of your child’s progress in the development areas, but appointments are needed.  If you live in the North Wayne School District call 618-673-3044 to make an appointment for your preschooler.

title: WOMANS CONFERENCE
full_story:
The Southeastern Illinois Regional Women’s Conference will take place on Friday, April 17th, at the Brubeck Arts Theater at Wabash Valley College in Mt. Carmel.  This regional event brings together women from across Southeastern Illinois for a day of inspiration, professional development, and meaningful connections.

Hosted through a collaboration of several area chambers, including the Flora Chamber of Commerce, Wabash County Chamber, Wayne County Chamber, Carmi Chamber, Lawrence County Chamber, Albion Area Chamber, Robinson Chamber, and Richland County Chamber, the conference is designed to empower women in business, leadership, and the community.

Attendees can expect an engaging experience focused on personal growth, professional development, and networking with women from across the region.  Events like this provide valuable opportunities to learn from others, share experiences, and build relationships that support both individual and community success.

If you would like to attend the conference or learn more about sponsorship opportunities, please reach out to the Flora Chamber of Commerce.

Tickets are $50 per person.  Includes breakfast, boxed lunch, goodie bag, and presentation.  Student Tickets are $20.

title: MUSGRAVE PLEADS GUILTY
full_story:
Joshua I. Musgrave, 48, of Geff, plead guilty to methamphetamine possession Tuesday in Wayne County Court and had nine other counts dismissed in the plea agreement with the state.  A 180-day stint at the Wayne County Jail was stayed.

All charges, including six alleged felonies and four alleged misdemeanors, were brought against Musgrave in September 2024.  Charges dismissed included two counts of felony theft and burglary, operating a non-highway vehicle, driving on a suspended license, possession of drug paraphernalia and contributing to the neglect of a minor.

Associate Judge Denton W. Aud gave Musgrave two years of conditional discharge and gave the defendant a no-contact order against three individuals: Royce Snell, John Kennedy and Jeanine Kennedy.

A restitution amount was also ordered for $1,000 to John Kennedy and $89 to the Wayne County Sheriff’s Department, and Judge Aud ordered Musgrave to pay $3,619 in fines and fees.

title: ISP SEIZED 100 lbs METH
full_story:
The Illinois State Police arrested a Wisconsin man in McLean County for allegedly trafficking meth on Monday.

Ivan Kuckuk, 25 of Madison, Wisconsin, was arrested for methamphetamine trafficking during a traffic stop on Interstate 74 near Bloomington just before 1 pm, according to an Illinois State Police news release.

While searching the vehicle, deputies allegedly located 99.7 pounds of suspected methamphetamine.  The estimated street value is over $500,000.

Illinois State Police report Kuckuk was the only person in the vehicle and was taken into custody without incident.

The McLean County State’s Attorney’s Office has also charged Kuckuk with methamphetamine trafficking.  He remains in the McLean County Jail pending his first court appearance.

title: DEERE SETTLES
full_story:
Deere & Co. agreed to pay $99 million as part of a settlement that would resolve a class action lawsuit accusing the farm equipment giant of monopolizing repair services.

The Moline, Illinois-based manufacturer, which does business under the John Deere brand, has faced a handful of “right to repair” complaints over the years.  The deal announced Monday, which still needs final approval from the court, would settle a 2022 lawsuit that accused the company of withholding repair software and conspiring with authorized dealers to force farmers to use their services for repairs, when they could otherwise fix tractors and other equipment themselves or use independent alternatives.

The plaintiffs alleged that meant Deere and its dealers could charge higher, “supracompetitive” prices and reap benefits from an “unlawfully restrained” market, per court filings.

Deere has continued to deny any wrongdoing, and maintained Monday it’s dedicated to supporting customers’ ability and access needed to repair their equipment.  But the company agreed to the settlement “to move forward and remain focused on what matters most; serving our customers,” Denver Caldwell, vice president of aftermarket and customer support, said in a statement.

Under the proposed agreement, filed in federal court in Illinois, the $99 million would go into a settlement fund for class members who paid Deere or its authorized dealers for large agriculture equipment repairs between January 10th, 2018 until the date of the deal’s preliminary approval.

The company also agreed to additional injunctive relief, aimed at strengthening the availability of repair resources and things like diagnostic checks.

Beyond this case, Deere still faces separate litigation from the Federal Trade Commission.  The FTC sued Deere in January 2025, at the end of the Biden administration, accusing the company of “unfair practices that have driven up equipment repair costs for farmers while also depriving farmers of the ability to make timely repairs.”  Deere at the time said the claims were baseless.

“Right to repair” calls have piled up across sectors over the years, particularly as technology found its way into more and more products workers and consumers rely on.  Beyond farm equipment, makers of goods like smartphones and video game consoles have also been accused of withholding tools or creating software-based locks that prevent even simple updates, unless they’re done by a shop authorized by the company; in turn, hampering independent repair businesses.  Under public pressure, lawmakers in several states have tried to combat this.
